## The idea

Sound C, E, and G together, then remove one note at a time. Without E, the chord
no longer tells you clearly whether it is major or minor. Without G, it loses
much of the stable frame around the other two pitches. Three notes can therefore
carry a surprisingly compact harmonic identity, with each member contributing
different information.

A *triad* contains a root and two notes stacked a third apart. For the moment,
count those thirds in semitones: a major third spans four and a minor third spans
three. Stack 4 then 3 for a major triad, 3 then 4 for minor, two 3s for diminished,
or two 4s for augmented. Writing the qualities as step arrays lets one constructor
make all four while keeping the audible difference close to the changed numbers.

## Run this

```{.ruby audio=""}
use_bpm 84
use_synth :piano

define :make_triad do |root, thirds|
  [root, root + thirds[0], root + thirds[0] + thirds[1]]
end

define :play_both_ways do |notes|
  play_chord notes, release: 1.2
  sleep 2
  notes.each do |pitch|
    play pitch, release: 0.45
    sleep 0.5
  end
  sleep 1
end

qualities = {
  major: [4, 3],
  minor: [3, 4],
  diminished: [3, 3],
  augmented: [4, 4]
}

qualities.each do |name, thirds|
  triad = make_triad(note(:c4), thirds)
  puts "#{name}: #{triad}"
  play_both_ways triad
end

puts "matches Sonic Pi: #{make_triad(60, [4, 3]) == chord(:c4, :major).to_a}"
```

Major and minor differ only at the middle pitch in this common-root comparison,
so listen there first. The diminished triad compresses both thirds and closes
its outer frame to a tritone. The augmented triad expands both and overshoots the
stable perfect fifth. Each chord sounds first as a block, where the tones fuse,
and then as an arpeggio, where you can trace the two stacked intervals.

## Change one thing

1. Move the root from `:c4` to `:a3`. Every pitch receives the same offset, so
   the chord changes register and name without changing quality. Follow the
   spacing rather than the absolute notes.
2. Reverse `[4, 3]`. This makes the lower third smaller and the upper third
   larger, turning major into minor while retaining the same seven-semitone
   outer frame.
3. Change to `:prophet` and lengthen the release. As neighbouring arpeggio notes
   overlap, the separate intervals begin to fuse into a chord; the attacks still
   reveal the order in which it was built.

## Why it works

The root acts as a reference address. The first third is an offset from it; the
second is an offset from the middle note. Cumulative addition turns those local
distances into playable pitches. This is the same operation used to build a
scale, reduced to three notes and two larger steps.

Quality changes the outer interval as well as the inner arrangement. Major and
minor both span a perfect fifth, seven semitones from root to top. Diminished
contracts that frame to the six-semitone tritone from Lesson 19. Augmented opens
it to eight. That is why the altered thirds affect the chord's stability, not
merely a vague shade of colour.

Semitone arrays do leave information behind. A written triad is also a stack of
letter-name thirds; enharmonic spellings that share piano keys need not explain
the same harmonic structure. This constructor deliberately works at the sounding
pitch layer. When a chord enters a key or printed score, retain its spelled root
and quality beside the generated integers so later notation code does not have
to guess how each pitch acquired its role.

The built-in `chord(:c4, :major)` call supplies a reference case for the local
constructor. A reusable version should compare the remaining qualities as well.
Passing those array checks shows that the pitch arithmetic agrees; auditioning
still has another job, since syntax and equality say nothing about whether a
chosen synth or release makes the contrasts easy to hear.

## Take it further

Build a ten-trial drill from the four entries in `qualities`. Begin with
`use_random_seed 42`; choose a quality and a root from MIDI 48 through 59, play
the arpeggio and then the block, leave four beats for an answer, and print the
name. Keep synth, rhythm, amplitude, and register span identical across trials.
That consistency removes clues unrelated to interval structure and makes a tally
of confusions useful evidence about what you can hear.
